passage:
Dear Ojas,

I know this week has been awful, with the job news and everything. I wanted to say something properly, so here's a letter.
At the café on Tuesday, when you looked so low, I asked, "Can I give you a hug?" and you said, "I'd rather not, sorry." I want you to know I wasn't offended at all. You once told me your family isn't huggy, and that's completely fine. Everyone's comfortable with different things.
So instead, I'm leaving a box of your favourite samosas at your door with this. And I'll keep Sunday free for a walk by the lake, if you'd like company.
I'm in your corner, hug or no hug.

Alka

qa.q: What is Alka leaving at Ojas's door?
qa.a: Alka is leaving a box of Ojas's favourite samosas with the letter.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when Ojas said no to the hug?
qa.a: Alka wasn't offended at all and understood, because different people are comfortable with different things.

qa.q: What did Alka handle wisely?
qa.a: Alka asked before hugging, accepted the no without offence and found other ways to show warmth, like samosas and a walk.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Ojas would likely feel relieved and cared for, knowing the no was respected and that Alka is still in Ojas's corner.

grounding: It shows a caring person asking before a hug, accepting a no without offence, and showing warmth in other ways that respect family habits.

passage:
You want the hug story, Tejas? Fine. Saurabh the hugger, that was me. I used to hug everyone. My family is like that. So at the office party last year, when our new colleague Deepa got her promotion, I just grabbed her. She went rigid and stepped back. Later a friend told me she's uncomfortable with touch from people she doesn't know well, and she had every right to be.
I felt terrible. I apologised, and she was gracious about it.
Since then I ask. "Hug? High-five? Nothing?" Most people laugh and pick one. Some say no, and that's fine.
And you, man. When I met you, you told me hugging wasn't done much in your home growing up. So we do the fist bump. Honestly, it's become our thing.

qa.q: What does Saurabh now ask people before touching them?
qa.a: Saurabh asks, "Hug? High-five? Nothing?"

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel after Deepa stepped back?
qa.a: Saurabh felt terrible and embarrassed, realising the hug wasn't welcome.

qa.q: What did Saurabh change after the office party?
qa.a: Saurabh started asking first, accepting a no, and finding other signs of warmth like the fist bump with Tejas.

qa.q: How might Deepa have felt when she was grabbed?
qa.a: She likely felt uncomfortable and caught off guard, which is why she went rigid and stepped back.

grounding: It shows a person learning to ask before hugging, accept a no without offence and respect how history and upbringing shape comfort with touch.

passage: I sit across from Chetan at work, so I saw this last Thursday. Anirban came back from a phone call looking grey. His father had been taken to hospital. People gathered around, and one colleague moved to hug him. Anirban stepped back, arms crossed. Chetan saw it. When the others went, Chetan went over and asked, quietly, 'Would a hug help, or would you rather not?' Anirban shook his head. 'Not a hugger. Sorry.' Chetan said, 'No sorry needed,' and went and made two cups of tea. He put one on Anirban's desk and sat next to him, not saying much, until Anirban was ready to leave. I don't know what Anirban was thinking. But when he left, he squeezed Chetan's shoulder briefly on his way out.

qa.q: What did Chetan make and bring to Anirban?
qa.a: Two cups of tea.

qa.q: What does Chetan seem to feel when Anirban steps back from the hug?
qa.a: Chetan seems concerned and attentive, noticing Anirban's discomfort and wanting to help in a welcome way.

qa.q: What did Chetan do that showed respect and warmth?
qa.a: He asked before hugging, accepted the no without offence and showed care with tea and quiet company instead.

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt when Chetan simply sat beside him?
qa.a: He probably felt supported without being crowded, which his brief shoulder squeeze suggests.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's account, someone asking before offering a hug, accepting a no and finding other ways to show warmth.

passage:
Friday: At Varun's farewell from the office, Jyoti threw her arms round him without thinking. He went rigid and stepped back, smiling awkwardly. Jyoti felt her face burn.
Saturday: She messaged him. 'Sorry about yesterday. I should have asked.' He replied, 'Thanks for saying that. In my family we don't really hug. And after some things growing up, I'm careful about it. Nothing to do with you.'
The following Friday: They met for coffee before he left the city. When they said goodbye, Jyoti asked, 'Hug, handshake or wave?' Varun grinned. 'Handshake, with feeling.' They shook hands warmly, and he said, 'That meant a lot, you asking.'

qa.q: What did Jyoti do at Varun's farewell?
qa.a: She threw her arms round him without thinking.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when Varun stepped back?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, with her face burning.

qa.q: What did Jyoti change the following Friday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She asked 'Hug, handshake or wave?', which let Varun choose and made the goodbye feel warm and safe.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt when Jyoti asked first?
qa.a: He felt respected and touched, saying it meant a lot.

grounding: Shows a caring person learning to ask before hugging, accepting a no without offence and finding another warm way to say goodbye.

passage: Ayesha, beti, you're sulking because your new friend won't hug you back? Let your Devika Khala tell you something. When I was your age, I had a friend at work called Farzana. Whenever I hugged her, she went stiff as a board. I was hurt. I thought she didn't like me. For months I kept hugging her, thinking she'd warm up. Then one day she told me, very quietly, that in her home touching was rare, and that some old things made hugs frightening for her. I felt terrible. I had never asked. After that I always asked, 'Hug or no?' Mostly she said no. So instead I brought her cutting chai every morning and saved her a seat. She came to my wedding and cried. We're still friends, forty years later.

qa.q: What did Devika bring Farzana every morning?
qa.a: Cutting chai.

qa.q: How did young Devika feel when Farzana stiffened at hugs?
qa.a: She felt hurt and thought Farzana did not like her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Devika's story?
qa.a: Farzana explaining why hugs were hard, after which Devika always asked first and showed warmth in other ways.

qa.q: How might Farzana have felt when Devika kept hugging her?
qa.a: Farzana probably felt uncomfortable and even frightened, but unsure how to say so.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a person learning to ask before hugging, accepting a no, and finding other ways to show warmth shaped by a friend's history.

passage: The train to Siliguri was delayed three hours, and the platform at Howrah was a wall of noise. Devika had just hung up after hearing her grandfather was in hospital, and her face had gone blank. Dolma put her arms out, then stopped halfway. "Can I hug you? Or is that too much right now?" Devika shook her head. "Not right now. Sorry." "Don't be sorry." Dolma dropped her arms and sat on their suitcase instead, making room. She bought two cups of chai from the vendor, held one out, and kept her shoulder close without touching. For a while they said nothing. Then Devika started talking about her grandfather's garden, and Dolma just listened, nodding, through three more announcements.

qa.q: How long was the train delayed?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: How did Devika seem to feel after the call, and what shows it?
qa.a: She seemed shocked and overwhelmed; her face had gone blank and she didn't want to be touched.

qa.q: How did Dolma show warmth after Devika said no?
qa.a: She accepted it without offence, made room on the suitcase, brought chai, stayed close without touching and listened.

qa.q: What would have changed if Dolma had hugged Devika without asking?
qa.a: Devika might have felt crowded and even more overwhelmed, and less free to say what she needed.

grounding: Shows a caring friend asking before a hug, accepting a no without offence and finding other ways to show warmth on a noisy, delayed platform.
